rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - one-season (2021) field experiment on processing tomato at Shihezi, Xinjiang, with aerated vs non-aerated mulched drip irrigation and two N rates, three replicates. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 - aerated irrigation had highly significant effects on yield, IWUE and NPFP; A1N2 gave the highest yield (32.05 t/ha), 23.69% above A0N1; aeration increased yield per plant and single fruit weight. Q4: Sections 3.1, 3.5 and Figure 8 - soil nutrient contents (SOC, DOC, TN, NH4-N, NO3-N) and C/N cycling gene abundances were measured under aeration and a path analysis linked them to yield (NO3-N direct path coefficient -1.047, C cycling genes 0.924). Q9: Table 3 - yield, IWUE and NPFP reported as mean +/- standard deviation (e.g. 32.05 +/- 0.40).
rows.notes: Supports the yield part of the claim only; crop quality was not measured. Q4 is borderline: soil nutrients/genes were measured and modelled as mediators, but soil oxygen/root hypoxia, the proposed mechanism of aeration, was only asserted (citing Western et al.). Q3 no: single harvest-weighing method. Q7: the recommendation of combining aeration with 270 kg/ha N reflects a significant AxN interaction and is phrased as a recommendation, not a stated requirement. Q8: no limitations stated. One site, one soil, one crop, one season.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - own field experiment with aerated vs non-aerated drip irrigation and two N rates on processing tomato in 2021.
rows.notes: The study does not measure pesticide use, pest or disease incidence; Section 2.2 states pesticide applications were applied uniformly across all plots as standard practice. It reports soil nutrients, GHG emissions, C/N cycling gene abundance, yield, IWUE and NPFP. No evidence for reduced pesticide applications under aerated drip irrigation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - one-season (2021) replicated field experiment on processing tomato with aerated vs non-aerated mulched drip irrigation and two N rates. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 - aerated irrigation significantly increased yield, yield per plant, IWUE and NPFP; A1N2 yielded 32.05 t/ha, 23.69% above A0N1. Q4: Sections 3.1, 3.5 and Figure 8 - soil nutrient contents and C/N cycling gene abundances measured under aeration and linked to yield by path analysis (NO3-N and C cycling genes with the largest direct effects). Q9: Table 3 - yield and IWUE given as mean +/- standard deviation.
rows.notes: Study uses Venturi air injection (ADI), not micro-nano bubble water; it supports the crop performance part of the passage for ADI. Q4 borderline as in row 03 (mediators measured but soil oxygen not). Single site, soil, crop and season; no triangulation; no stated limitations; combination with 270 kg/ha N is a recommendation rather than a stated requirement.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - own 2021 field experiment with aerated vs non-aerated drip irrigation on sandy loam in Xinjiang. Q2: Section 3.1 and Figure 4 - aeration increased SOC and DOC (by 1.75-10.94% and 3.21-3.30%) and NH4-N (7.75-14.44%) in the 0-40 cm layer; Abstract and Conclusion state aerated irrigation increased SOC, DOC, TN and NH4-N. Q9: Figure 4 caption - bars represent standard deviation of the mean (n = 3).
rows.notes: Evidence for improved soil condition is mixed: Section 3.1 also reports aeration reduced TN and NO3-N by 11.39% and 20.00%, and Section 3.3 reports aeration increased N2O, CO2, CH4 and total GHG emissions (6.21-6.73%). Q4 no: the mechanism (improved root-zone aeration/porosity) is asserted with citation, not measured; gene abundances are outcomes rather than the mediating variable for the nutrient effect. Single method, single site/soil/crop/season, no stated limitations, no requirement stated for the effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a one-year (2021), single-site, replicated plot experiment on processing tomato under mulched drip irrigation with Venturi aeration (A0/A1) and two N rates (N1/N2), measuring soil nutrients, GHG emissions, C/N cycling functional genes, yield, IWUE and NPFP. Note the Abstract gives N2 as 270 kg/ha while the Discussion mentions 240 kg/ha for A1N2, an internal inconsistency.
